$comment: Declarative readiness evidence for the Manna progress report.
Why a hand-maintained file rather than inference: the statuses below are
CLAIMS, and a claim needs named evidence and a reviewer. Deriving them
automatically would mean guessing — and a dashboard that guesses
'VERIFIED' is worse than no dashboard, because it manufactures exactly
the false confidence the audit record exists to prevent.
So every entry carries an `evidence` string, and changing a status is a
reviewable diff in a pull request. Anything not actually checked is
NOT RUN or BLOCKED, never VERIFIED.
Permitted status values: VERIFIED, PARTIAL, BLOCKED, NOT RUN,
NOT APPLICABLE. No percentages — there is no defined denominator, so a
verifiedAgainstCommit: master at e0f3f0d, the tip after Sprint 1's five pull requests were merged on 2026-10-26: #69 -> 1bc81df, #68 -> ce7255a, #67 -> a08c82f, #71 -> 0b609f4, #70 -> e0f3f0d. Suite measured on that tree: 61 files / 907 tests passing, typecheck 0 errors, lint 0 errors / 28 warnings. All four required checks are green on e0f3f0d and are now ENFORCED by ruleset 25851827. Rows describe master unless a row names a PR. The previous version of this line read '6927ebd' and 'five unmerged branches', which the merges made false.

operational.name: Database backup and restore verification
operational.evidence: PROCEDURE VERIFIED SYNTHETICALLY, PRODUCTION REHEARSAL NOT RUN (PR #70). The Phase 0 runbook was executed end to end against a synthetic production-shaped database on 2026-10-25: pg_dump/pg_restore exit 0 with zero stderr in 0.20s; verify-migrate.sql zero non-OK rows; source and target row counts identical; reconciliation-check.sql 7/7 PASS non-vacuously; the application suite passed against the restored database; teardown left nothing behind. Negative cases confirm the checks can fail: a dropped column is caught by step 2, unequal payment legs fail 3 of 7 reconciliation checks, and the privilege probe reports 114 unreachable objects with no grants and 0 with the full set. Evidence: docs/audits/2026-10-25-restore-rehearsal-synthetic.md. What remains NOT RUN is everything production-only: backup availability, recovery point, real restore duration (0.20s on a trivial dataset is not transferable), and production ownership and privileges. Phase 0 is NOT complete.

operational.name: Redis-backed rate limiting in production
operational.evidence: CONFIGURATION CONFIRMED, OPERATION NOT VERIFIED. The owner reports REDIS_URL is set for production (2026-10-20, name only; no value requested or held by this session). That is not the same claim as "limits are shared": lib/rate-limit.ts falls back to in-process counters on any Redis client or command failure. The RAW EXCEPTION is deliberately not logged because it can embed the credential-bearing URL; a degradation line naming the stage and a cumulative count is emitted to stderr, so a signal exists but carries no connection detail. The degradation itself IS caller-visible — allowed and remaining change, and a caller spreading requests across instances can exceed the nominal limit; what is missing is an explicit backend-failure signal. A failure no longer latches: it sets redisDownUntil, which suppresses Redis attempts for a 30s cooldown and then retries, so an instance recovers on its own instead of counting in-process until it recycles. rateLimitBackendHealth() reports activeBackend, cooldown state and the cumulative degradation count, with no credential in it. (An earlier version of this row described the old permanent redisUnavailable latch; that variable no longer exists.) Operational proof needs POST /api/admin/operations/redis-rate-limit run against production with an authenticated admin session holding the exceptions:manage permission — SuperAdmin or OperationsAdmin; a lesser admin role gets 403, which is easy to misread as Redis being down. That route performs an isolated set/get/delete and is already implemented and audited. ONE POST PROVES ONLY THE INSTANCE THAT SERVED IT: the backend state and the in-process counters are module-level in lib/rate-limit.ts, therefore per serverless instance, so another live instance can still be counting in-process while this one answers pass. Serverless instances cannot be addressed individually, so repeated POSTs give sampling confidence rather than coverage; VERIFIED requires evidence covering every live instance, or equivalent deployment-wide evidence, which in practice means monitoring the degradation signal rather than an operator running the route by hand. Nothing external scrapes that signal yet. Row therefore stays PARTIAL on a passing POST.

operational.name: Secret scanning in CI
operational.evidence: VERIFIED 2026-10-26. Gitleaks 8.21.2 runs on every PR into master over full history, pinned by version and verified against a published SHA256, with --redact and SARIF commitMessage stripping; it succeeded on master at e0f3f0d. The single reason this row was PARTIAL — "the check is not enforced by branch protection, so a detection would not block a merge" — no longer holds: secret scan is one of the four contexts required by ruleset 25851827. Scope note kept: the .gitleaks.toml allowlist is keyed on exact synthetic literals rather than on paths, so a real credential later pasted into an allowlisted file is still caught.

operational.name: Static analysis (CodeQL) in CI
operational.evidence: VERIFIED 2026-10-26. CodeQL security-extended runs on every PR into master and weekly, with least-privilege permissions and security-events: write isolated from the job running the test suite; analyze javascript-typescript succeeded on master at e0f3f0d. The single reason this row was PARTIAL — not enforced by branch protection — no longer holds: it is one of the four contexts required by ruleset 25851827. VERIFIED here means the control runs and gates, not that the codebase is free of defects CodeQL cannot see.

operational.name: Branch protection enforcing required checks
operational.evidence: VERIFIED 2026-10-26 by reading the rulesets API. The owner acted on the instructions recorded in the previous version of this row (which read BLOCKED). Ruleset 25851827, "master CI and security checks": enforcement active, target branch, conditions include refs/heads/master with no excludes, bypass_actors EMPTY, and one required_status_checks rule with strict_required_status_checks_policy true requiring exactly the four intended contexts — install · typecheck · lint · test · build; dependency audit; secret scan; analyze javascript-typescript. So the checks are enforced AND a PR must be up to date with master before merging. Two deliberate limits on the claim: the ruleset contains ONLY required_status_checks, so there is no required-review rule and no force-push restriction, and a direct push to master that passes CI is not blocked by it; and the CLASSIC protection API still answers 403 to this environment, so a protected:false reading taken from that endpoint reflects this session's token rather than the absence of protection — the ruleset is the authority. All five Sprint 1 PRs were merged through these required checks.

operational.name: GitHub Actions supply-chain pinning
operational.evidence: VERIFIED — PR #68 merged 2026-10-26 as ce7255a (this row previously read ENGINEERING COMPLETE, UNMERGED). Every uses: reference in .github/workflows now names a 40-hex commit SHA with the human-readable tag in a trailing comment. Measured on the merged tree by listing every uses: that does NOT match @[0-9a-f]{40}: the list is empty. lib/__tests__/workflow-action-pinning.test.ts enforces it on every run and its matchers tolerate YAML-quoted keys — an earlier version of those regexes did not, and would have read straight past a quoted unpinned entry. Mutation-checked: reintroducing a mutable tag fails the test. What pinning does NOT do is verify what is inside a pinned SHA; it removes tag mutability, not trust in the action.

operational.name: Production dependency advisories
operational.evidence: MASTER FIXED AND ENFORCED, DEPLOYMENT STILL UNVERIFIED, DEV CHAIN OPEN. master carried next@16.3.8 with three open advisories — two unauthenticated RCE (Image Optimization; `use cache` typed arrays, GHSA-673q-mjm6-r5xr) and one DoS (GHSA-p3m5-59mp-jv5r) — all patched in >=16.4.1. PR #69 merged 2026-10-26 as 1bc81df; measured on the merged tree at e0f3f0d, package.json declares next 16.4.3 and pnpm-lock.yaml resolves next@16.4.3, so master is fixed. Audit measured on that tree: production dependencies report NO known vulnerabilities (pnpm audit --prod), while the full tree including dev reports 24 advisories — 2 critical, 13 high, 8 moderate, 1 low — all in the dev chain (e.g. vitest > @vitest/mocker, GHSA-qxg6-89mg-rqv8). ci.yml fails the build only on production-dependency criticals and highs and reports the dev chain advisory-only; that is a documented tier split, NOT a suppression, and the 24 are recorded here as open rather than clean. PARTIAL for two independent reasons: the RUNNING DEPLOYMENT is not confirmed to have rebuilt from 1bc81df or later (403 CONNECT to both api.vercel.com and the deployment host from this environment, re-confirmed 2026-10-26), and the dev-chain advisories are unresolved. The structural gap also persists: nothing watches an unchanged tree — see the Dependabot row.

operational.name: Dependabot alerts enabled
operational.evidence: BLOCKED ON OWNER ACTION, proven by attempt rather than inferred. GET /repos/Carl-cab/carls-way/dependabot/alerts and GET /repos/Carl-cab/carls-way/vulnerability-alerts BOTH answer HTTP 403 to this session, re-confirmed 2026-10-26. A 403 means this token may not read the setting — it is NOT evidence that alerts are disabled, and it is not a clean scan; the state is genuinely UNKNOWN from here and is recorded as blocked rather than guessed. This matters because it is the only durable backstop for the failure that has now happened twice: both the next advisory set and the follow-redirects one five days earlier reached master AFTER its last green CI run, and each was found only because an unrelated PR happened to re-run the audit. CI cannot detect an advisory disclosed against an unchanged tree. Owner action, two minutes, no secret involved: GitHub → repository Settings → Advanced Security (or Code security and analysis) → enable Dependency graph, then Dependabot alerts, and optionally Dependabot security updates; then report whether the alert list is non-empty. A scheduled dependency scan has been prepared on branch ci/scheduled-dependency-scan (daily, workflow_dispatch, contents: read + issues: write, opens one deduplicated issue on failure, and treats an unreachable advisory service as a FAILURE rather than a pass). It is NOT part of Sprint 1's authorized five PRs and awaits separate authorization; it is a complement to Dependabot, not a substitute, because it reads the same advisory source CI already reads.

ownerActions.action: Compare two production requests to settle header trust
ownerActions.why: Send TWO production requests and report, for each, clientIdentity().source AND whether the resolved id EQUALS the forged value that request supplied — a boolean, never the id and never the IP. Request A sends no IP headers. Request B supplies a distinctive forged value in x-real-ip, x-forwarded-for and x-vercel-forwarded-for. The source name alone does NOT answer this: if both requests select x-vercel-forwarded-for the name is identical whether the platform overwrote the forged value or passed it through, so only the equality tells you which happened. If B's id equals what B sent, the header is attacker-controlled and every limit keyed on it is per-attempt, not per-client. PR #71 documents the question; this environment cannot answer it (403 CONNECT to both api.vercel.com and the deployment host).

ownerActions.action: Decide the money-bucket policy on Redis loss (recommendation ready)
ownerActions.why: A recommendation is written up in docs/decisions/0007-money-bucket-policy-on-redis-loss.md, reviewed against master at 0b609f4 (lib/rate-limit.ts is byte-identical at e0f3f0d): KEEP ALL THREE FAIL-OPEN — money:send 20/h, money:split-pay 30/h, money:transfer-execute 10/h, all keyed on the authenticated user id, so header loss cannot collapse them. Reasoning, corrected: fail-closed turns a Redis outage into a TOTAL customer-visible payments outage while the database, providers and application are all healthy; fail-open keeps the per-user limit in force on every instance and loosens the aggregate ceiling for the subset of users actively abusing the system during the window. TWO CLAIMS WERE WITHDRAWN from an earlier version of this row and of the decision record, because review was right that neither was supportable. (1) It said fail-open costs 'a single-digit multiplier'. The fallback is limit × instances and NOTHING IN THIS REPOSITORY ESTABLISHES THE INSTANCE COUNT — no deployment limit, no observed count — and this environment cannot obtain one (403 CONNECT to api.vercel.com and the deployment host). Treat the multiplier as UNBOUNDED until someone with deployment access establishes a concurrency ceiling. (2) It cited the per-intent idempotency key as a constraint on abuse. It is not: it prevents one intent being debited twice and says nothing about a caller creating many separate intents. The only control that survives a Redis outage and actually caps volume is velocity_checks. The recommendation still stands because it rests on the asymmetry of the two failure modes — a certain outage for everyone versus a loosened limit for attackers — which does not depend on the multiplier's size. What the unknown size does change is the urgency of ask 3. The asks: (1) scrape rateLimitBackendHealth(), which nothing does, so a silent demotion to per-instance counting is today indistinguishable from normal operation; (2) alert on sustained degradation with a named owner; (3) move these three counters to PostgreSQL, which the application cannot run without anyway, removing the dilemma instead of choosing a side. Nothing is implemented either way; this needs your decision.
